title: Can I Trust This Health Claim?

zones.label: Evidence
zones.summary: Ask whether the claim is supported by checkable research or only a dramatic story.
facts: Testimonials are experiences, not proof that a product works for everyone.
Specific, verifiable evidence is stronger than vague science-sounding language.
Compare the basic fact across more than one reliable source.

zones.label: Expertise
zones.summary: Check whether the source has relevant training and can be held accountable.
facts: A title matters only when it matches the health topic.
Anonymous authors and unnamed experts are difficult to verify.
Reliable organizations explain who reviewed the information.

zones.label: Sales Motive
zones.summary: Notice who benefits if you believe the claim or buy the product.
facts: Advertising is a sales message, not neutral evidence.
Urgency, fear, and miracle promises are warning signs.
Independent evidence matters when the source profits from the conclusion.

zones.label: Recency
zones.summary: Check when information was published or updated and whether guidance may have changed.
facts: Old information is not automatically false, but some health guidance changes.
A screenshot may hide its original date and context.
Current official guidance is useful for changing topics.

zones.label: Personal Fit
zones.summary: Ask whether the advice fits the person, family, culture, condition, and situation.
facts: General information cannot diagnose an individual.
A trusted adult or appropriate professional can help apply evidence safely.
A choice can be evidence-based and still need adaptation.

quiz.question: Which bay separates research from testimonials?
Which bay checks training and accountability?
Which bay asks who profits if you believe the claim?
Which bay checks publication and update dates?
Which bay asks whether general advice suits a particular person and context?
